The external ear is the part you can see (the auricle) and the canal leading to the eardrum. It collects sound and directs it inwards.
The external ear consists of the auricle, a plate of elastic cartilage covered with skin, and the external acoustic meatus, about 2.5 cm long, ending at the tympanic membrane.
A blow to the auricle can cause a haematoma between cartilage and perichondrium; untreated, it can lead to 'cauliflower ear'.
The tympanic membrane, or eardrum, is a thin membrane at the end of the ear canal. Sound makes it vibrate.

The tympanic membrane separates the external acoustic meatus from the middle ear. It is oval, about 1 cm across, and slightly cone-shaped, with the handle of the malleus attached to its inner surface.
On examination with an otoscope a normal membrane is pearly grey with a cone of reflected light; it can perforate after infection or trauma, causing conductive hearing loss.
The malleus (hammer) is the first and largest of the three tiny bones of the middle ear, attached to the eardrum.
Its handle is attached to the tympanic membrane and its head articulates with the incus in the epitympanic recess.
Transmits vibrations of the tympanic membrane to the incus. The tensor tympani inserts on it and damps loud sounds.
The incus (anvil) is the middle of the three small bones of the middle ear, linking the malleus and the stapes.
Its body articulates with the head of the malleus; its long process articulates with the head of the stapes.
Transmits vibrations from the malleus to the stapes.
The stapes (stirrup) is the smallest bone in the body. Its footplate rocks in the oval window, passing sound into the inner ear.
Its head articulates with the incus; its footplate fits into the oval window of the inner ear, held by an annular ligament.

Together the ossicles and the area difference between the tympanic membrane and the oval window amplify sound pressure about 20-fold, matching air to the fluid of the inner ear. The stapedius inserts on it and damps loud sounds.
In otosclerosis the footplate becomes fixed by new bone, causing conductive hearing loss.
The tensor tympani is a tiny muscle in the middle ear that tightens the eardrum to protect the ear from loud sounds.
It lies in a bony canal above the auditory tube and inserts on the handle of the malleus. Supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3).
The stapedius is the smallest skeletal muscle in the body. It steadies the stapes and protects the inner ear from loud sounds.
It arises within the pyramidal eminence of the middle ear and inserts on the neck of the stapes. Supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
Facial nerve lesions proximal to the nerve to stapedius cause hyperacusis: ordinary sounds seem uncomfortably loud.
The bony labyrinth is a set of fluid-filled channels in the temporal bone. Its snail-shaped cochlea is for hearing; its vestibule and three semicircular canals are for balance.

The bony labyrinth lies in the petrous part of the temporal bone and consists of the cochlea, the vestibule and the three semicircular canals (anterior, posterior and lateral), containing perilymph and the membranous labyrinth.

Hair cells in the cochlea convert sound vibrations into nerve signals; those in the semicircular ducts detect rotation of the head and those in the utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and head position.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, the commonest cause of vertigo, is caused by loose otoconia in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior one.
The round window is a small membrane-covered opening between the middle ear and the cochlea. It bulges out as the stapes pushes in, letting the inner-ear fluid move.
It lies on the medial wall of the middle ear below the oval window and is closed by the secondary tympanic membrane.
The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression. It also carries taste from the front of the tongue and controls tears and some saliva.

The facial nerve (CN VII) leaves the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, enters the internal acoustic meatus with the vestibulocochlear nerve, runs through the facial canal in the temporal bone (giving the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani) and leaves the skull at the stylomastoid foramen to divide within the parotid gland.

Motor to the muscles of facial expression, stapedius and posterior belly of digastric; taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani); parasympathetic to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.

A lower motor neuron lesion (for example Bell palsy) paralyses the whole of one side of the face; an upper motor neuron lesion (stroke) spares the forehead because the forehead receives cortical input from both hemispheres.
The cochlear nerve carries hearing signals from the cochlea to the brainstem.
It is the auditory part of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII); its fibres arise from the spiral ganglion in the cochlea and pass through the internal acoustic meatus to the cochlear nuclei.
A vestibular schwannoma in the internal acoustic meatus typically presents with one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus.
The vestibular nerve carries balance signals from the inner ear to the brainstem.
It is the balance part of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII); its fibres arise from the vestibular ganglion and supply the semicircular ducts, utricle and saccule.
Inflammation of the nerve (vestibular neuritis) causes sudden severe vertigo without hearing loss.
The bony part of the nasal septum is the back of the wall that divides the nose into two sides.
It is formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below, continuous anteriorly with the septal cartilage.
The cartilaginous part of the nasal septum is the flexible front part of the wall between the two sides of the nose.
It is formed mainly by the septal cartilage, which joins the bony septum posteriorly.
The anterior septum (Little's area, Kiesselbach plexus) is the commonest site of nosebleeds.
The soft palate is the soft, muscular back part of the roof of the mouth. It rises when you swallow to stop food entering the nose.
The soft palate hangs from the posterior edge of the hard palate and ends in the uvula; the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches pass from it to the tongue and pharynx.
Elevated and tensed during swallowing and speech to close off the nasopharynx. Its muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus), except tensor veli palatini (mandibular nerve).
With a vagus nerve lesion the uvula deviates away from the affected side when the patient says 'ah'.
The incisors are the eight flat front teeth (four upper, four lower) used for cutting food.
Each quadrant of the permanent dentition has a central and a lateral incisor. Incisors have a single root and a chisel-shaped crown.
Cutting and biting. Upper incisors are supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve (from CN V2), lower incisors by the inferior alveolar nerve (from CN V3).
The canines are the four pointed teeth at the corners of the mouth, used for tearing food.
One canine in each quadrant, with the longest root of any tooth; the upper canine root reaches towards the side of the nose.
The premolars are the eight teeth between the canines and the molars, used for crushing and grinding.
Two premolars in each quadrant of the permanent dentition; they replace the deciduous molars and usually have one or two roots and two cusps.
The molars are the large back teeth used for grinding food. This model shows the first and second molars; the third molars (wisdom teeth) are not included.
Up to three molars in each quadrant; upper molars usually have three roots and lower molars two. The roots of the upper molars lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
Impacted third molars are common; removal of lower third molars risks injury to the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves.
